title: A Glowing Green Cloud, Seen From Space
summary: A satellite photo has captured something strange and beautiful off the coast of Canada: a giant underwater cloud that seems to glow green beneath the waves. The cloud is about 4 miles long, and it appeared during a Pacific herring spawning event in Barkley Sound, along the southern coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia. The photo was taken on February 19, 2026, by the Landsat 9 satellite. The green cloud is made of milt, a fluid containing sperm that male fish release to fertilize eggs. Pacific herring reproduce by gathering in large groups. The females lay eggs, which stick to kelp, sea grasses and rocky surfaces, before the males release their milt over the area. Herring, which grow to around 10 inches long, often gather in this spot in late winter or early spring, staying for several weeks before releasing their reproductive cells. The cloud looks green in the images, but the milt itself is actually white. It appears green only because it sits closer to the surface than the surrounding seafloor, so less of the reflected light is absorbed by the water. The same effect is why shallow patches of water often look turquoise from above. The coastline near Salmon Beach is perfect for herring to spawn because it hits what scientists call a sweet spot. Biologist Jessica Moffatt said herring prefer spawning spots that are protected, have a rocky bottom and have lower salt levels in the water. Barkley Sound has all three. The herring are an important species here. They are a main food source for Chinook salmon, which give Salmon Beach its name, and they are also fished by local First Nation groups.
why_it_matters: Satellite photos let scientists watch huge ocean events from space, helping them protect fish that feed salmon, whales and people.
